summary: Supply the total cholesterol, the triglycerides and the low-density lipoprotein and the LDL cholesterol calculator solves for high-density lipoproteins (HDL). It is built for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the LDL cholesterol calculator work?
sections.html:
The LDL cholesterol calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports high-density lipoproteins (HDL) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the total cholesterol, the triglycerides (TG) and the low-density lipoprotein (LDL).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the LDL cholesterol calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

High-density lipoproteins (HDL)=-low-density lipoprotein (LDL) − 1 ÷ 5 × triglycerides (TG) + total cholesterol

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Total cholesterol = 10 Mg/d l, Triglycerides (TG) = 10 Mg/d l and Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) = 10 Mg/d l. Working through the relationship above gives High-density lipoproteins (HDL) = -2 Mg/d l.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: High-density lipoproteins (HDL) = -2 Mg/d l should be roughly the size you expected from Total cholesterol = 10 Mg/d l and Triglycerides (TG) = 10 Mg/d l.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in milligrams per deciliter, and convertible to any of the 2 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Cholesterol – for HDL or LDL, opening in milligrams per deciliter
  • Cholesterol – for HDL or LDL, opening in milligrams per deciliter
  • Cholesterol – for triglycerides, opening in milligrams per deciliter
  • Cholesterol – for HDL or LDL, opening in milligrams per deciliter

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The LDL cholesterol calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the total cholesterol, the triglycerides and the low-density lipoprotein — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the LDL cholesterol calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the LDL cholesterol calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns high-density lipoproteins (HDL), derived from the total cholesterol, the triglycerides and the low-density lipoprotein. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the LDL cholesterol calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the total cholesterol, the triglycerides and the low-density lipoprotein, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter total cholesterol in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Total cholesterol opens in milligrams per deciliter and the chip beside it offers 2 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports High-density lipoproteins (HDL) = -2 Mg/d l. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the LDL cholesterol calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
